newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Swiss jobless rate hits record 5.7 percent.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Swiss jobless rate hits record 5.7 percent.

text.p: Swiss unemployment jumped to a record 5.7 percent in January as seasonal factors accentuated the stagnant economy's inability to generate new jobs, officials said on Monday.

Economists said the leap in the number of jobless from 5.3 in December would prompt the Swiss National Bank (SNB) to continue its generous monetary policy, but few expected it to cut the discount rate, already at a historic low of 1.0 percent.

The Federal Office of Trade, Industry and Labour (BIGA) in Berne said the jobless rolls grew by 13,330 to stand at 205,501 at the end of January, fulfiling the BIGA forecast last month that the 200,000-person mark would soon be crossed.
"Seasonal factors came through in full force," BIGA chief Jean-Luc Nordmann told reporters in Berne, noting for example that 7,500 more construction workers were idle than in November.

Changes in Swiss labour law also expanded the number of registered unemployed by around 3,000 people, he added, worsening an already bleak picture painted by the weak economy that has essentially stagnated since 1990.
"To help out, the Swiss National Bank has to continue its loose monetary policy," Nordmann said.

He also called for speeding up planned tax reform to help boost the prospects of small and mid-sized companies and said employers and workers had to pull together to make the labour market more flexible.
Credit Suisse Group economist Thomas Heller said the jobless rate could climb to six percent in March and April.
"It is conceivable that the National Bank would then react and perhaps cut the discount rate by a quarter point," he said.
Other economists thought this unlikely, even though the SNB has made clear it will maintain the generous monetary policy it adopted in mid-1995 until there are clear signs the economy is picking up.
SNB chairman Hans Meyer has stuck to his forecast that gross domestic product will rise 0.5 percent this year, helped by the impact of a weaker Swiss franc on exports.
Union Bank of Switzerland analyst Alexander Kobler said he thought the SNB would keep policy steady.
"The SNB will probably not become even more expansive. There is some leeway for money market rates to come down, but we do not expect a discount rate cut," he said.

Unemployment, traditionally below one percent when the Swiss economy was riding high, rose to an average 4.7 percent last year as the strong Swiss franc and slow domestic demand prompted many companies to streamline operations.

"Even if the unemployment numbers stabilise or even decline slightly in the spring and in the summer, the average joblessness level will be between 15,000 and 20,000 higher than last year before we can anticipate a slight decline in 1998," BIGA said last month.

Weak demand from Switzerland's main trading partners, especially in Europe, have hobbled the export-dependent Swiss economy, but so have protectionist attitudes and cartel-like practices among all but the largest companies, economists say.
The economy is widely estimated to have contracted by around 0.75 percent last year.
